studies.title: L-citrulline modulates pancreatic enzyme activity and biochemical markers in adult female Wistar rats with metabolic syndrome.
studies.abstract:
Background

Metabolic syndrome (MetS) induces profound pancreatic damage characterised by oxidative stress and chronic inflammation.

Objectives

This study investigated the protective effects of L-citrulline (L-CIT) in the pancreas of a MetS animal model by evaluating oxidative stress responses, inflammatory cytokines, interferon gamma (IFN-γ), aldose reductase (AKR1B1), glucose kinase-3β, abdominal fat and body weight.

Methods

The animals (Wistar rats; Rattus norvegicus) were divided into five groups (n = 6), three of which received MetS induction via a 20% fructose solution and received oral L-CIT at escalating doses (200, 400, or 800 mg/kg). Group 1 served as the normal control, while group 2 served as the negative control (20% fructose solution). Post-treatment, pancreas samples were collected for biochemical analysis to determine the dose-dependent effects of L-CIT.

Results

Pancreatic oxidative stress was significantly reduced (P< 0.05) in the L-CIT-treated groups vs the MS-untreated group. TNF-ɑ, IL-1β and IL-6 were significantly reduced (P< 0.05) with L-CIT treatment vs the MS-untreated group. However, IL-10 was significantly increased (P < 0.05) in the L-CIT group compared with the MS-untreated group. Pancreatic IFN-γ was significantly (P< 0.05) reduced in the L-CIT groups compared to the MS-untreated group, whereas the changes in pancreatic BDNF were not statistically significant. Both pancreatic AKR1B1 and GSK-3β were significantly reduced (P< 0.05) in the groups given L-CIT vs the MS-untreated group. Abdominal fat and body weight were significantly lower (P< 0.05) in the L-CIT groups than in the MS-untreated group.

Conclusion

L-CIT holds promise as a therapeutic supplement for preserving pancreatic health in metabolic disease.

studies.title: Maternal dietary citrulline supplementation increases fetal growth and programs pancreatic development in the lambs.
studies.abstract: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), caused by maternal undernutrition, impairs fetal growth and increases the risk for postnatal metabolic dysfunction. L-arginine can mitigate these effects; however, its use in sheep is limited by ruminal microbial degradation. Interestingly, L-citrulline, the precursor for arginine synthesis, bypasses ruminal catabolism and may be a practical alternative. This study evaluated if maternal L-citrulline supplementation to nutrient restricted ewes from gestational days (GD) 28 to 140 (term = 147) enhances fetal growth in lambs. Gestating ewes were fed 50% of National Research Council (NRC) nutritional recommendations to induce IUGR and received either L-citrulline (0.40% of diet) or an isonitrogenous alanine control (0.61% of diet). Birth weight and pre-suckling blood samples were collected, and lambs remained with dams until postnatal day 60 (PND60) (citrulline: n = 13; alanine: n = 10). Lambs from L-citrulline treated ewes were heavier at birth (P = 0.05) and PND60 (P < 0.05), with greater (P < 0.05) absolute weights of the pancreas, brain, liver, and small intestine. Pancreatic mass per gram of body weight was greater (P < 0.05) in citrulline lambs. The relative proportion of endocrine and exocrine pancreas were not different between treatments. Circulating insulin concentrations were greater (P = 0.05) at birth and circulating glucose concentrations were increased (P < 0.05) in the citrulline lambs on PND60. These results suggest that maternal L-citrulline supplementation is a viable alternative to arginine for improving fetal growth during maternal malnutrition, with benefits persisting through weaning.

studies.title: Lactobacillus murinus alleviates insulin resistance via promoting L-citrulline synthesis.
studies.abstract:
Aims

The role of Lactobacillus murinus as a potential probiotic is being explored. Our objectives were to explore the effects of Lactobacillus murinus on insulin resistance and the underlying mechanism.

Methods

Insulin resistance animal models were applied to study the effect of L. murinus and the underlying mechanism by six weeks of treatment. Metformin was administered in vitro to analyze the growth and metabolites of L. murinus. Serum metabolites were further analyzed after L. murinus administration. The effect of L-citrulline and the underlying mechanism in alleviating insulin resistance were evaluated.

Results

L. murinus not only reduced body weight gain and postprandial blood glucose (PBG) but improved impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and insulin resistance. Moreover, L. murinus inhibited the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors (IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α) while promoted the secretion of anti-inflammatory factor (IL-10). Further, L. murinus promoted the expression of carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1 (CPT1) while inhibited phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK) and glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase). A total of 147 metabolites of L. murinus were identified, in which the content of L-citrulline increased to 7.94 times after metformin regulation. Further, the serum concentration of L-citrulline significantly increased after L. murinus administration. Similarly, L-citrulline reduced body weight gain and PBG, improved IGT and insulin resistance. Additionally, L-citrulline improved inflammation, promoted CPT1 while inhibited PCK and G6Pase.

Conclusions

L. murinus mediated by L-citrulline alleviated insulin resistance via promoting fatty acid oxidation and inhibiting gluconeogenesis, suggesting that supplementation of L. murinus could be a potential therapeutic approach for type 2 diabetes related to insulin resistance.

studies.title: Dietary Supplementation with L-Citrulline Between Days 1 and 60 of Gestation Enhances Embryonic Survival in Lactating Beef Cows.
studies.abstract: Low fertility limits reproductive efficiency in cattle. This study was conducted with multiparous Brangus cows receiving dietary supplementation with or without L-citrulline [Cit; an immediate precursor of L-arginine (Arg)]. During the entire experimental period, cows grazed green pasture and had free access to drinking water and mineral blocks. One hundred and seven (107) cows were assigned randomly to one of three treatment groups: dried distillers grains with solubles (DDGS) without Cit supplement (n = 36); DDGS top-dressed with rumen-protected Cit product (RPAA; n = 36); or unprotected Cit product (RUAA; n = 35). After 2 months of lactation, all cows were synchronized to estrus and were bred once via artificial insemination. From Day 1 to Day 60 of gestation, cows were individually fed once daily 0.84 kg of a supplement (DDGS; control), 0.56 kg of DDGS plus 0.28 kg of RUAA (containing 0.07 kg of unencapsulated Cit), or 0.56 kg of DDGS plus 0.28 kg of RPAA (containing 0.07 kg of rumen-protected Cit). The supplemental dose of Cit was equivalent to 0.5% of the estimated daily intake of 14 kg dry matter from pasture. On Days 40 and 60 of gestation, ultrasound was used to determine pregnancy rates. Each pregnant cow had a single conceptus. On Day 60 of gestation, blood samples were obtained from the jugular vein. All cows grazed normally and appeared healthy. Birth rates for live-born calves were 22% and 35% in cows receiving DDGS alone and Cit supplementation, respectively (p < 0.05). The beneficial effect of Cit was associated with increases in concentrations of Cit (+19%), Arg (+20%), ornithine (+19%), proline (+17%), and insulin (+82%) but decreases in concentrations of ammonia (-14%) in maternal plasma (p < 0.05). Thus, dietary supplementation with Cit is a simple, novel, and cost-effective nutritional method to increase the reproductive efficiency of lactating beef cows.

studies.title: Sex- and Dose-Dependent Effect of L-Citrulline on Body Weight and Food Intake in Obese Type 2 Diabetic Rats.
studies.abstract:
Background

Obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are associated with nitric oxide (NO) deficiency. L-citrulline (Cit), a substrate for NO synthesis, has been suggested as a treatment for obesity and T2D.

Objectives

This study aims to determine the effects of Cit on body weight, food intake, and water consumption in obese T2D male and female rats.

Methods

The T2D was induced using a high-fat diet (HFD) and a low dose of streptozotocin (STZ). Obese male (n = 30) and female (n = 30) rats with T2D were divided into five groups (n = 6/group) that received Cit (0, 1, 4, 7, and 10 g/L in drinking water for 8 weeks). Body weight, food intake, and water consumption were measured every week. Serum Cit and nitrite+nitrate (NOx) concentrations were measured at weeks 0, 4, and 8, and serum fasting glucose was measured at week 8.

Results

Compared to non-treated T2D rats, Cit-treated male rats had lower body weight (11.3%, 13.0%, and 11.6% at doses of 4, 7, and 10 g/L), lower food intake (4.7% and 5.5% at doses of 4 and 7 g/L), and water consumption (7% at dose 7 g/L). In female rats, Cit decreased body weight (7.2%, 8%, and 7.3% at doses of 4, 7, and 10 g/L), food intake (4.0% and 5.0% at doses of 4 and 7 g/L), and water consumption (5% and 6.6% at doses of 4 and 7 g/L; all P < 0.001). The body weight and food intake-lowering effects of Cit were higher in T2D male rats than females (all P < 0.05), but decreased water consumption was comparable between sexes. A Cit dose of 7 g/L was most effective in reducing all measured parameters in both sexes.

Conclusions

The Cit decreased body weight, food intake, and water consumption in obese T2D male and female rats. These effects were sex- and dose-dependent.

studies.title: Anti-obesity and anti-diabetic effects of L-citrulline are sex-dependent.
studies.abstract: Anti-diabetic and anti-obesity effects of L-citrulline (Cit) have been reported in male rats. This study determined sex differences in response to Cit in Wistar rats. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) was induced using a high-fat diet followed by low-dose of streptozotocin (30 mg/kg) injection. Male and female Wistar rats were divided into 4 groups (n = 6/group): Control, control+Cit, T2D, and T2D + Cit. Cit (4 g/L in drinking water) was administered for 8 weeks. Obesity indices were recorded, serum fasting glucose and lipid profile were measured, and glucose and pyruvate tolerance tests were performed during the Cit intervention. White (WAT) and brown (BAT) adipose tissues were weighted, and the adiposity index was calculated at the end of the study. Cit was more effective in decreasing fasting glucose (18 % vs. 11 %, P = 0.0100), triglyceride (20 % vs. 14 %, P = 0.0173), and total cholesterol (16 % vs. 11 %, P = 0.0200) as well as decreasing gluconeogenesis and improving glucose tolerance, in females compared to male rats with T2D. Following Cit administration, decreases in WAT weight (16 % vs. 14 % for gonadal, 21 % vs. 16 % for inguinal, and 18 % vs. 13 % for retroperitoneal weight, all P < 0.0001) and increases in BAT weight (58 % vs. 19 %, for interscapular and 10 % vs. 7 % for axillary, all P < 0.0001) were higher in females than male rats with T2D. The decrease in adiposity index was also higher (11 % vs. 9 %, P = 0.0007) in females. The anti-obesity and anti-diabetic effects of Cit in rats are sex-dependent, with Cit being more effective in female than male rats.

studies.title: Effect of Various Pathological Conditions on Nitric Oxide Level and L-Citrulline Uptake in Motor Neuron-Like (NSC-34) Cell Lines.
studies.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal motor neuron disorder that causes progressive paralysis. L-Citrulline is a non-essential neutral amino acid produced by L-arginine via nitric oxide synthase (NOS). According to previous studies, the pathogenesis of ALS entails glutamate toxicity, oxidative stress, protein misfolding, and neurofilament disruption. In addition, L-citrulline prevents neuronal cell death in brain ischemia; therefore, we investigated the change in the transport of L-citrulline under various pathological conditions in a cell line model of ALS. We examined the uptake of [<sup>14</sup>C]L-citrulline in wild-type (hSOD1wt/WT) and mutant NSC-34/ SOD1<sup>G93A</sup> (MT) cell lines. The cell viability was determined via MTT assay. A transport study was performed to determine the uptake of [<sup>14</sup>C]L-citrulline. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis was performed to determine the expression levels of rat large neutral amino acid transported 1 (rLAT1) in ALS cell lines. Nitric oxide (NO) assay was performed using Griess reagent. L-Citrulline had a restorative effect on glutamate induced cell death, and increased [<sup>14</sup>C]L-citrulline uptake and mRNA levels of the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1) in the glutamate-treated ALS disease model (MT). NO levels increased significantly when MT cells were pretreated with glutamate for 24 h and restored by co-treatment with L-citrulline. Co-treatment of MT cells with L-arginine, an NO donor, increased NO levels. NSC-34 cells exposed to high glucose conditions showed a significant increase in [<sup>14</sup>C]L-citrulline uptake and LAT1 mRNA expression levels, which were restored to normal levels upon co-treatment with unlabeled L-citrulline. In contrast, exposure of the MT cell line to tumor necrosis factor alpha, lipopolysaccharides, and hypertonic condition decreased the uptake significantly which was restored to the normal level by co-treating with unlabeled L-citrulline. L-Citrulline can restore NO levels and cellular uptake in ALS-affected cells with glutamate cytotoxicity, pro-inflammatory cytokines, or other pathological states, suggesting that L-citrulline supplementation in ALS may play a key role in providing neuroprotection.

studies.title: Maternal citrulline supplementation enhances placental function and fetal growth in a rat model of IUGR: involvement of insulin-like growth factor 2 and angioge
studies.abstract: To determine the effects of maternal citrulline supplementation on fetal growth and placental efficiency in a rat model of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) induced by maternal protein restriction. Pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to three groups: NP (receiving a control 20% protein diet), LP (a 4% protein diet), or LP-CIT (an LP diet along with L-citrulline, 2 g/kg/d in drinking water). On the 15th and 21st day of gestation (GD15 and GD21, respectively), dams underwent a C-section, by which fetuses and placentas were extracted. The expression of genes involved in placental growth and angiogenesis was studied by quantitative RT-PCR. Maternal citrulline supplementation increased fetal weight at GD21, and fetal weight/placental weight ratio, an index of placental efficiency, from mid gestation (p < 0.001). The expression of Igf2-P0, a placenta-specific variant of insulin-like growth factor 2 (Igf2) gene, and Vegf and Flt-1, involved in angiogenic pathways, was enhanced in the LP-CIT group (versus NP, p < 0.001, p < 0.01, and p < 0.05 for Igf2-P0, Vegf, and Flt-1, respectively). In a model of IUGR induced by protein deprivation, citrulline enhances fetal growth, placental efficiency, and the expression of genes involved in angiogenesis. The relevance of such effect in human pregnancies complicated by IUGR warrants further study.

studies.title: L-Citrulline Improves IGF-1 Signaling Pathway in Preeclampsia via Polyamines.
studies.abstract:
Background

Preeclampsia is a severe pregnancy complication with no effective pharmacological therapy available. We previously demonstrated that L-citrulline supplementation improves preeclampsia phenotypes in Dahl salt-sensitive rats, an animal model of superimposed preeclampsia. This study aimed to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Methods

Pregnant Dahl salt-sensitive rats were treated with L-citrulline. In addition, patients with preeclampsia were recruited to donate placenta and serum samples.

Results

In patients with preeclampsia, the placental IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) expression was significantly reduced compared with healthy pregnancy, associated with a downregulation of ZEB1 (zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1) and an upregulation of miR-486-5p and miR-210. L-citrulline supplementation in preeclampsia rats significantly increased the placental expression of IGF-1 and ZEB1 and reduced the expression of miR-486-5p and miR-210. Total serum polyamine level was reduced in patients with preeclampsia and pregnant Dahl salt-sensitive rats, while L-citrulline treatment maintained the serum polyamine level in Dahl salt-sensitive rats during pregnancy. Placental IGF-1 expression was positively correlated to serum polyamine levels. Moreover, both L-citrulline and polyamines normalized the expression of IGF-1 and some antiangiogenic markers in cultured human placental vascular endothelial cells treated with preeclampsia serum. Results from IGF-1 siRNA experiments indicate that part of the L-citrulline effects on gene expression was dependent on IGF-1.

Conclusions

L-citrulline supplementation improves the IGF-1 signaling pathway in preeclampsia, at least partly, via polyamine production. Maternal supplementation with L-citrulline or polyamine may represent a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for preeclampsia.

studies.title: Effects of Citrulline Supplementation on Exercise Performance in Humans: A Review of the Current Literature.
studies.abstract: Gonzalez, AM and Trexler, ET. Effects of citrulline supplementation on exercise performance in humans: A review of the current literature. J Strength Cond Res 34(5): 1480-1495, 2020-L-citrulline, a nonessential amino acid found primarily in watermelon, has recently garnered much attention for its potential to augment L-arginine bioavailability, nitric oxide production, and exercise performance. Over the past decade, L-citrulline has received considerable scientific attention examining potentially ergogenic properties for both aerobic and anaerobic exercise performance. Thus, the purpose of this article is to summarize the theoretical rationale behind L-citrulline supplementation and to comprehensively review the available scientific evidence assessing the potential ergogenic value of L-citrulline supplementation on vascular function and exercise performance in humans. In addition, research that has investigated the potential synergistic effects of L-citrulline with other dietary ingredients (e.g., arginine, antioxidants, nitrates, and branched-chain amino acids) is reviewed. Oral L-citrulline and citrulline malate supplementation have shown to increase plasma citrulline and arginine concentrations, along with total nitrate and nitrite concentrations. Although blood flow enhancement is a proposed mechanism for the ergogenic potential of L-citrulline, evidence supporting acute improvements in vasodilation and skeletal muscle tissue perfusion after supplementation is scarce and inconsistent. Nevertheless, several studies have reported that L-citrulline supplementation can enhance exercise performance and recovery. Given the positive effects observed from some investigations, future studies should continue to investigate the effects of both acute and chronic supplementation with L-citrulline and citrulline malate on markers of blood flow and exercise performance and should seek to elucidate the mechanism underlying such effects.

studies.title: Malate or Not? Acute Effects of L-Citrulline Versus Citrulline Malate on Neuromuscular Performance in Young, Trained Adults: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo
studies.abstract: L-citrulline (CIT) supplementation seems to improve resistance training performance; yet, whether malate has additive ergogenic effects when combined with CIT is unknown. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial aimed to compare the acute effects of CIT versus citrulline malate (CMA) supplementation on neuromuscular performance and exertion and emotional perceptions in young, trained men and women. 43 (21 women; 24.2 ± 3.7 years) participants ingested a placebo, CIT (5.3 g of CIT), or CMA (5.3 g of CIT, 2.7 g of malate) 45 min before three experimental sessions in a counterbalanced manner. We evaluated the upper and lower limb maximal neuromuscular and ballistic performance through the two-point method and countermovement jump. Strength-endurance was assessed across three sets of 10 repetitions in the squat and bench press exercises. Exertion and emotional perceptions were evaluated before and after the assessment and during the strength-endurance assessment. CIT and CMA supplementation did not enhance maximal neuromuscular performance (all p ≥ .061, ηp2≤.066), or ballistic strength (all p ≥ .348, ηp2≤.025). Neither CIT nor CMA supplementation improved strength-endurance as observed in the total number of repetitions (all p ≥ .590, ηp2≤.013), repetitions before reaching velocity loss threshold (all p ≥ .623, ηp2≤.010), mean velocity (all p ≥ .792, ηp2≤.004), mean velocity decline (all p ≥ .293, ηp2≤.029), and mean velocity maintenance (all p ≥ .393 ηp2≤.022), or exertion and emotional perceptions (both p ≥ .306, ηp2≤.028). In conclusion, CIT and CMA supplementation may not increase the neuromuscular performance during low- to moderate-volume resistance training sessions in young, trained adults. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (No. NCT05183893).

studies.title: Acute Effect of L-Citrulline Supplementation on Resistance Exercise Performance and Muscle Oxygenation in Recreationally Resistance Trained Men and Women.
studies.abstract: L-citrulline serves as a nitric oxide precursor with the potential to increase blood flow and improve resistance exercise performance, yet more research is needed to examine its ergogenic potential. To examine the effect of L-citrulline supplementation on resistance exercise performance, muscle oxygenation, and the subjective perception of effort, energy, focus, fatigue, and muscle pump, eighteen resistance-trained men (n = 11) and women (n = 7) (21.4 ± 1.8 years; 172.3 ± 7.5 cm; 76.9 ± 10.8 kg) were randomly assigned for supplementation with 8 g of L-citrulline (CIT) or a placebo (PL) in a cross-over fashion one hour prior to testing. Participants completed an isometric mid-thigh pull test (IMTP), a ballistic bench press protocol [two sets of two repetitions at 75% 1-repetition maximum (1 RM) with maximum ballistic intent], and a strength-endurance bench press protocol [five repetition-maximum sets at 75% 1RM]. Barbell velocity and power were measured via a linear position transducer during the ballistic protocol, while the repetitions completed, volume load and muscle oxygenation were quantified during the strength-endurance protocol. Subjective measures were assessed at the baseline and immediately pre- and post-exercise. Repeated measures of the analysis of variance and Bayesian equivalents revealed no significant interactions, providing evidence favoring the null hypothesis (BF10 < 1) for IMTP (PL 497.5 ± 133.6 vs. CIT 492.5 ± 129.4 N), barbell velocity, and power, and repetitions completed (PL 36.7 ± 7.2 vs. CIT 36.9 ± 8.1 repetitions). There were also no significant interactions for muscle oxygenation parameters or subjective measures except perceived fatigue. Women reported greater fatigue across all time points compared to men (~1.88 au, p = 0.045, BF10 = 0.2). The results indicate that a single 8 g dose of L-citrulline did not enhance isometric force production, muscle endurance, or muscle oxygenation parameters during the protocol implemented in this study.

studies.title: Combined L-Citrulline Supplementation and Slow Velocity Low-Intensity Resistance Training Improves Leg Endothelial Function, Lean Mass, and Strength in Hyperten
studies.abstract: Hypertension is highly prevalent in postmenopausal women. Endothelial dysfunction is associated with hypertension and the age-related decreases in muscle mass and strength. L-citrulline supplementation (CIT) and slow velocity low-intensity resistance training (SVLIRT) have improved vascular function, but their effect on muscle mass is unclear. We investigated whether combined CIT and SVLIRT (CIT + SVLIRT) would have additional benefits on leg endothelial function (superficial femoral artery flow-mediated dilation (sfemFMD)), lean mass (LM), and strength in hypertensive postmenopausal women. Participants were randomized to CIT (10 g/day, n = 13) or placebo (PL, n = 11) alone for 4 weeks and CIT + SVLIRT or PL + SVLIRT for another 4 weeks. sfemFMD, leg LM and muscle strength were measured at 0, 4, and 8 weeks. CIT increased sfemFMD after 4 weeks (CIT: Δ1.8 ± 0.3% vs. PL: Δ−0.2 ± 0.5%, p < 0.05) and 8 weeks (CIT + SVLIRT: Δ2.7 ± 0.5% vs. PL + SVLIRT: Δ−0.02 ± 0.5, p = 0.003). Leg LM improved after CIT + SVLIRT compared to PL + SVLIRT (Δ0.49 ± 0.15 kg vs. Δ0.07 ± 0.12 kg, p < 0.05). Leg curl strength increased greater with CIT + SVLIRT compared to PL + SVLIRT (Δ6.9 ± 0.9 kg vs. Δ4.0 ± 1.0 kg, p < 0.05). CIT supplementation alone improved leg endothelial function and when combined with SVLIRT has additive benefits on leg LM and curl strength in hypertensive postmenopausal women.

studies.title: One Week of L-Citrulline Supplementation Improves Performance in Trained Cyclists.
studies.abstract: Stanelle, ST, McLaughlin, KL, and Crouse, SF. One week of L-citrulline supplementation improves performance in trained cyclists. J Strength Cond Res 34(3): 647-652, 2020-L-citrulline (CIT) is a nonessential amino acid that is touted as an ergogenic aid for athletic performance because of its purported ability to stimulate nitric oxide production. Although previous research has demonstrated that CIT supplementation over a period of days improves physiological factors such as V[Combining Dot Above]O2 kinetics, no studies to date have explored whether there is a direct benefit to endurance performance. This study used a randomized, double-blind, crossover design to test whether chronic supplementation with pure CIT improves cycling performance over a maltodextrin placebo (PLAC). Nine trained male cyclists (24 ± 3 years; 181 ± 7 cm; 76 ± 13 kg; 4.18 ± 0.51 L·min V[Combining Dot Above]O2max) completed two 7-day supplementation periods (6 g·d of CIT or PLAC) separated by a 7-day washout. Subjects consumed the final 6-g dose 2 hours before the cycling performance evaluation, which consisted of a 40-km time trial (TT) followed by a supramaximal sprint repeat task (SRT). Paired t-tests and repeated-measures analysis of variance (α = 0.05) were used to analyze TT and SRT data, respectively. CIT supplementation produced an improvement in TT time of 5.2% that trended toward significance (p = 0.08). Furthermore, CIT promoted a significant increase in average heart rate, average rating of perceived exertion, and average power throughout the TT (p < 0.05). However, supplementation with CIT did not prevent fatigue during the SRT. Overall, this study is the first to demonstrate that CIT supplementation may provide a modest improvement to endurance cycling performance in trained athletes.

studies.title: Impact of L-citrulline supplementation and whole-body vibration training on arterial stiffness and leg muscle function in obese postmenopausal women with high b
studies.abstract: Aging is associated with increased arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity, PWV) and muscle strength/mass loss. Exercise training alone is not always effective to improve PWV and lean mass (LM) in older women. To investigate the independent and combined effects of whole-body vibration training (WBVT) and L-citrulline supplementation on PWV and muscle function in women, forty-one postmenopausal women aged 58 ± 3 years and body mass index (34 ± 2 kg/m(2)) were randomly assigned to the following groups: WBVT, L-citrulline, and WBVT + L-citrulline for 8 weeks. WBVT consisted of four leg exercises three times weekly. Aortic (cfPWV) and leg (faPWV) PWV, leg LM index, leg strength, and body fat percentage (BF%) were measured before and after the interventions. WBVT + L-citrulline decreased cfPWV (-0.91 ± 0.21 m/s, P < 0.01) compared to both groups. All interventions decreased faPWV (P < 0.05) similarly. Leg LM index increased (2.7 ± 0.5%, P < 0.001) after WBVT + L-citrulline compared with L-citrulline. Both WBVT interventions increased leg strength (~37%, P < 0.001) compared to L-citrulline while decreased BF% (~2.0%, P < 0.01). Reductions in cfPWV were correlated with increases in leg LM index (r = -0.63, P < 0.05). Our findings suggest that leg muscle strength and arterial stiffness can be improved after WBVT, but its combination with L-citrulline supplementation enhanced benefits on aortic stiffness and leg LM. Therefore, WBVT + L-citrulline could be an intervention for improving arterial stiffness and leg muscle function in obese postmenopausal women with prehypertension or hypertension, thereby reducing their cardiovascular and disability risk.

studies.title: Diaphragm-specific effects of L-citrulline in mdx mice highlight its potential as adjuvant of standard therapy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
studies.abstract:
Background and purpose

The absence of the protein dystrophin in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) leads to progressive muscle weakness, failing regeneration and deregulation of nitric oxide (NO) signalling. We focused on L-citrulline, a precursor of L-arginine, required for NO production in muscle, which is reduced in dystrophic mdx muscle.

Experimental approach

L-Citrulline was administered (2 mg g-1 die-1), through diet, in comparison and/or in combination with prednisolone (1 mg kg-1, 5 days per week subcutaneously) to 4- to 5-week-old mdx mice for 8 weeks.

Key results

L-Citrulline increased the levels of L-arginine, L-citrulline and L-ornithine in plasma and quadriceps of mdx mice. L-citrulline, alone or plus prednisolone, significantly improved maximal forelimb force in vivo, while ameliorating diaphragm movement amplitude and reducing diaphragm echodensity. In parallel, ex vivo, we detected a significant improvement of diaphragm force and contraction kinetics in mice treated with L-citrulline alone or in combination with prednisolone. L-citrulline also restored the expression of genes involved in Ca2+ handling during contraction (RyR1, RyR3 and SERCA), while reducing the markers of inflammation and fibrosis (CD68 and TGFβ1) and ameliorating mitochondrial biogenesis-associated genes (PGC1-α and MEF2C). No effect was observed on S-nitrosylation levels of HDAC2 and on diaphragm and gastrocnemius nNOS gene expression, suggesting a NO-independent mechanism underlying the positive outcome observed.

Conclusions

Our results revealed the ability of L-citrulline supplementation to ameliorate in vivo and ex vivo function of diaphragm muscle, highlighting novel metabolic and calcium-related mechanisms of potential clinical interest.

explanation.what_it_is_line: An amino acid that helps your body make nitric oxide, a blood-vessel relaxer.
explanation.what_it_is: L-citrulline is a naturally occurring amino acid — a building block that your cells use to make proteins and other vital molecules. Your body produces it on its own, but it is also found in small amounts in foods like watermelon and pumpkin seeds. People typically take it as a supplement in powder or capsule form to boost the amount available in their bloodstream.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Converts to arginine, triggering nitric oxide release; nitric oxide widens blood vessels and improves blood flow.
explanation.how_it_works: When you take L-citrulline, your body converts it into another amino acid called L-arginine. L-arginine then activates an enzyme called eNOS (endothelial nitric oxide synthase) — think of it as a signaling switch — which produces nitric oxide. Nitric oxide is a chemical messenger that tells blood vessel walls to relax and widen, a process called vasodilation. Wider vessels mean blood flows more easily, delivering oxygen and nutrients to muscles and tissues. This improved blood flow is why citrulline is thought to enhance exercise performance, lower blood pressure, and support healthy circulation.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in trials; long-term and interaction data remain limited.
explanation.safety_detail: Published trials reported minimal side effects, most commonly mild gastrointestinal upset. However, most studies lasted weeks to a few months, so effects of prolonged use are not well characterized. No comprehensive drug-interaction studies were retrieved, and safety in certain populations (pregnancy, kidney disease, adolescents) remains untested or excluded from trials.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: not systematically studied in retrieved trials; unknown risk if combined with blood pressure meds or blood thinners
Pregnancy: excluded from most trials; a 2025 preeclampsia RCT (n=115) is an exception, but long-term pregnancy safety data are sparse
Kidney disease: not adequately tested in people with renal impairment; caution warranted since kidneys process amino acids
Adolescents: absent from retrieved trials; safety and efficacy in minors remain unknown
explanation.chem_meaning: L-citrulline is a small, water-loving amino acid (XLogP −4.3), meaning it dissolves readily in blood and is not trapped by fatty tissues. Its small size and polarity make it absorbed and transported efficiently across the intestinal barrier and into cells, allowing it to reach tissues quickly.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two independent meta-analyses (2019 and 2025) pooled results from multiple randomized trials and found L-citrulline supplementation lowered blood pressure by an average of about 4 mmHg (range roughly −6.5 to −1.5 mmHg). The 2025 meta-analysis included 415 participants; the 2019 analysis reviewed 424 participants. A 2026 trial in 66 healthy adults confirmed this effect was larger in people with pre-hypertension. Studies were conducted 2019–2026 and included healthy volunteers, middle-aged and older adults, and people with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two independently published meta-analyses converge on the same direction and magnitude of effect, indicating replicated synthesis. Pooled data from over 800 participants across multiple trials provide adequate statistical power and consistency.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 systematic review identified multiple randomized trials showing L-citrulline improved exercise performance metrics — chiefly endurance and time to exhaustion. Recent 2025 trials tested acute and short-term effects: one RCT (n=21) compared L-citrulline versus citrulline malate on neuromuscular performance in young people; another (n=15, 2025) combined L-citrulline with high-intensity interval training (HIIT) in obese adults; a third (2025) examined cerebrovascular function during sprint training. The 2026 post-COVID trial (n=43) also measured endothelial (blood-vessel) function alongside performance.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis exists but has not been independently replicated. Study quality and sample sizes vary; most trials are recent (2020–2026) and small to modest in scale. The direction of effect is consistent, but without a second independent meta-analysis pooling the same question, confidence is held at moderate pending further synthesis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only 3 human trials were retrieved (all 2025, mostly unpublished or in-press). Two randomized trials (one with n=15 obese adults, one with unspecified sample) measured blood glucose levels during or after L-citrulline supplementation; neither abstract reported conclusive glucose-lowering effects. Animal studies in rats (2025–2026) showed L-citrulline modulated pancreatic enzyme activity and improved insulin sensitivity via bacterial-derived citrulline synthesis. Human trials verified approximately 241 total participants, but most abstracts lacked sample-size details.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Very few human trials exist, and no pooled meta-analysis confirms they agree. Animal evidence is suggestive but does not automatically predict human outcomes. Human data remain preliminary and inconsistent, warranting moderate grade pending larger or replicated studies.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 systematic review identified trials on citrulline and muscle performance. Recent randomized trials (2022–2025) tested acute and 6-week effects: a 2025 RCT (n=21) compared L-citrulline to citrulline malate on neuromuscular measures; a 2023 RCT examined acute effects on resistance exercise and muscle oxygenation in recreationally trained people; a 2022 trial (n=13) combined L-citrulline with slow-velocity resistance training and found improvements in leg endothelial function. Verified sample sizes across 2 of 9 studies total only ~34 participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis exists but has not been independently verified. Verified human sample sizes are modest (~34 across published abstracts). The effect direction is consistent but the evidence base is small and not yet independently replicated, keeping grade at moderate.

explanation.evidence_base: The bulk of evidence is human and recent (2019–2026). Most trials are randomized and controlled, ranging from acute single-dose studies to 6-week interventions. Two independent meta-analyses support the blood-pressure finding, but other outcomes rely on single syntheses or scattered trials. Very few long-term studies (>3 months) or large-scale trials (>200 participants per arm) are visible in the retrieved records, meaning longer-term safety and efficacy remain less certain than short-term effects.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records show exercise performance and muscle strength have been studied only in healthy or recreationally active adults and people with post-COVID-19 syndrome; effectiveness in frail elderly, sedentary populations, or chronic disease remains untested in the available abstracts. Most studies last 6 weeks or less; safety and efficacy beyond 3 months are not well characterized in the provided data. Blood-sugar outcomes rest on only 3 human trials and inconsistent findings; whether citrulline truly improves glucose control in people with diabetes or prediabetes cannot yet be determined from these records. No retrieved trials assessed pregnancy, adolescence, or renal disease, leaving safety in these groups unknown.

appraisal.headline: Blood pressure evidence is solid with independent meta-analyses and ~839 verified participants; exercise performance, muscle strength, and blood sugar rest on small, heterogeneous trials with no pooled synthesis, making clinical claims premature for those outcomes.

concerns.issue: Exercise performance: no extractable pooled effect
concerns.detail: Despite 19 human RCTs, the engine notes 'pooled effect: none extractable.' A single 2020 systematic review exists but remains unreplicated and unverified. With median sample size of 15 and only 7 of 20 studies reporting n, individual trials are underpowered to detect clinically meaningful effects. The 2025 trial 'does not improve running performance in the heat' directly contradicts the claimed benefit.

concerns.issue: Muscle strength: sparse and unverified synthesis
concerns.detail: Only 9 studies total (8 human RCTs), with pooled effect 'none extractable.' Only 2 of 9 studies report sample sizes (n=13, n=21), yielding ~34 verified participants across the outcome. The engine flags this as 'imprecision: effect estimate may be unstable.' A single 2020 systematic review exists but no independent replication. Conclusions about muscle strength are built on a foundation of severe sample-size underreporting and single-synthesis dependence.

concerns.issue: Blood sugar: predominantly animal evidence with minimal human data
concerns.detail: Of 13 studies, 10 are animal models; only 2 are RCTs in humans, with total verified human n ~30 across them. The engine notes 'no pooled analysis confirms [studies] agree; held at moderate pending review.' Extrapolating from rat pancreatic enzyme activity and fetal growth in rodents to human glucose control is a large mechanistic leap. The human evidence is too sparse and animal-focused to support clinical claims.

concerns.issue: Blood pressure: outcome heterogeneity and responder variability not resolved
concerns.detail: While the 2025 and 2019 meta-analyses converge on mean difference of -4.02 mmHg, the 2026 RCT (n=66) explicitly notes 'vascular effects of l-citrulline supplementation in healthy adults are largely influenced by the pre[existing condition].' A 2026 trial states 'Compliance and Genetic Variability Are Determinants of the Success,' indicating substantial individual variation. The pooled estimate masks subgroups in whom the drug has little or no effect, and the evidence base does not clearly identify predictors of response.

concerns.issue: Systematic underreporting of sample sizes across all outcomes
concerns.detail: Across 70 studies in the evidence base, only 9–17 of 20–27 per outcome report sample size, leaving 50–75% of studies with n omitted from abstracts. The engine acknowledges 'true total is substantially larger' but cannot verify it. This opacity prevents independent assessment of whether the synthesized literature is adequately powered or subject to publication bias favoring positive small trials. Readers cannot evaluate the real precision of pooled estimates.

appraisal.mechanism_check: L-Citrulline → increased NO production → endothelial vasodilation → lower blood pressure is biologically coherent and supported by the blood pressure evidence (two meta-analyses, ~839 participants). However, the leap from NO bioavailability to exercise performance and muscle strength is weaker: NO improves blood flow, but whether this translates to measurable gains in resistance strength or aerobic work capacity in untrained or trained populations remains unclear from the retrieved RCTs. Blood sugar effects are purely animal-derived (pancreatic enzyme modulation, fetal programming), with no mechanistic bridge to human glycemic control demonstrated in the 2 small human RCTs.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: For exercise performance and muscle strength, a skeptic would note that the retrieved 16–19 RCTs show median n=13–21, no meta-analytic pooling exists for either outcome, and a 2025 trial explicitly *fails* to find improvement in running performance. The 'Moderate' grades rest on single, unreplicated systematic reviews written before most of the 2025–2026 data arrived. For blood sugar, 77% of evidence is animal work; the 2 human RCTs are tiny and underpowered. The 'Moderate' grade there is primarily a placeholder rather than a confidence statement. Overall, only blood pressure clears a high bar; the other three outcomes have been upgraded to match its prominence in marketing without equivalent empirical support.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: For exercise performance and muscle strength: a multi-center RCT with n≥150, pre-specified primary outcome (e.g., 1-RM leg press, time-to-exhaustion in trained subjects), and published protocol would resolve heterogeneity; alternatively, a registered meta-analysis with modern methods (e.g., risk-of-bias stratification, subgroup analysis by training status) could clarify the actual effect size. For blood sugar: a properly powered RCT (n≥200) in people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, measuring HbA1c as primary outcome over ≥12 weeks, would move the evidence from animal-dominated to human-based. For blood pressure, the picture is already reasonably clear; the next step is identifying predictors of responders (genetic, metabolic, baseline BP status) to move from population averages to precision medicine.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un aminoácido que ayuda a tu cuerpo a producir óxido nítrico, un relajante de los vasos sanguíneos.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La L-citrulina es un aminoácido que ocurre naturalmente — un bloque de construcción que tus células utilizan para producir proteínas y otras moléculas vitales. Tu cuerpo la produce por sí solo, pero también se encuentra en pequeñas cantidades en alimentos como la sandía y las semillas de calabaza. Las personas típicamente la toman como suplemento en forma de polvo o cápsula para aumentar la cantidad disponible en su torrente sanguíneo.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Se convierte en arginina, desencadenando la liberación de óxido nítrico; el óxido nítrico ensancha los vasos sanguíneos y mejora el flujo sanguíneo.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Cuando tomas L-citrulina, tu cuerpo la convierte en otro aminoácido llamado L-arginina. La L-arginina luego activa una enzima llamada eNOS (sintasa del óxido nítrico endotelial) — piénsalo como un interruptor de señalización — que produce óxido nítrico. El óxido nítrico es un mensajero químico que le dice a las paredes de los vasos sanguíneos que se relajen y se ensanchen, un proceso llamado vasodilatación. Los vasos más anchos significan que la sangre fluye más fácilmente, entregando oxígeno y nutrientes a los músculos y tejidos. Este flujo sanguíneo mejorado es por qué se cree que la citrulina mejora el rendimiento del ejercicio, reduce la presión arterial y apoya la circulación saludable.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerada en ensayos; los datos de largo plazo e interacciones permanecen limitados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos publicados reportaron efectos secundarios mínimos, siendo más comúnmente molestias gastrointestinales leves. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los estudios duraron semanas a pocos meses, por lo que los efectos del uso prolongado no están bien caracterizados. No se recuperaron estudios de interacción farmacológica integral, y la seguridad en ciertas poblaciones (embarazo, enfermedad renal, adolescentes) permanece sin probar o excluida de los ensayos.
safety_bullets: Interacciones farmacológicas: no estudiadas sistemáticamente en los ensayos recuperados; riesgo desconocido si se combina con medicamentos para la presión arterial o anticoagulantes
Embarazo: excluido de la mayoría de los ensayos; un ensayo aleatorizado de preeclampsia de 2025 (n=115) es una excepción, pero los datos de seguridad del embarazo a largo plazo son escasos
Enfermedad renal: no probado adecuadamente en personas con insuficiencia renal; se recomienda precaución ya que los riñones procesan aminoácidos
Adolescentes: ausentes de los ensayos recuperados; la seguridad y eficacia en menores de edad permanecen desconocidas
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La L-citrulina es un aminoácido pequeño y que ama el agua (XLogP −4.3), lo que significa que se disuelve fácilmente en la sangre y no queda atrapado por los tejidos grasos. Su pequeño tamaño y polaridad la hacen absorbida y transportada eficientemente a través de la barrera intestinal y hacia las células, permitiéndole llegar a los tejidos rápidamente.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dos metanálisis independientes (2019 y 2025) agruparon resultados de múltiples ensayos aleatorios y encontraron que la suplementación con L-citrulina redujo la presión arterial en un promedio de aproximadamente 4 mmHg (rango aproximadamente −6.5 a −1.5 mmHg). El metanálisis de 2025 incluyó 415 participantes; el análisis de 2019 revisó 424 participantes. Un ensayo de 2026 en 66 adultos sanos confirmó que este efecto era mayor en personas con prehipertensión. Los estudios se realizaron entre 2019–2026 e incluyeron voluntarios sanos, adultos de mediana edad y mayores, y personas con síndrome post-COVID-19.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Dos metanálisis publicados independientemente convergen en la misma dirección y magnitud de efecto, indicando una síntesis replicada. Los datos agrupados de más de 800 participantes en múltiples ensayos proporcionan potencia estadística adecuada y consistencia.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Una revisión sistemática de 2020 identificó múltiples ensayos aleatorios que mostraban que la L-citrulina mejoró las métricas de rendimiento del ejercicio — principalmente resistencia y tiempo hasta el agotamiento. Ensayos recientes de 2025 probaron efectos agudos y a corto plazo: un ensayo aleatorizado (n=21) comparó L-citrulina versus malato de citrulina en el rendimiento neuromuscular en personas jóvenes; otro (n=15, 2025) combinó L-citrulina con entrenamiento de intervalos de alta intensidad (HIIT) en adultos obesos; un tercero (2025) examinó la función cerebrovasular durante el entrenamiento de velocidad. El ensayo post-COVID de 2026 (n=43) también midió la función endotelial (de los vasos sanguíneos) junto con el rendimiento.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Un único metanálisis existe pero no ha sido replicado independientemente. La calidad del estudio y los tamaños de muestra varían; la mayoría de los ensayos son recientes (2020–2026) y pequeños a modestos en escala. La dirección del efecto es consistente, pero sin un segundo metanálisis independiente agrupando la misma pregunta, la confianza se mantiene moderada en espera de síntesis adicional.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo 3 ensayos humanos fueron recuperados (todos de 2025, en su mayoría no publicados o en prensa). Dos ensayos aleatorios (uno con n=15 adultos obesos, uno con muestra no especificada) midieron los niveles de glucosa en sangre durante o después de la suplementación con L-citrulina; ninguno de los resúmenes reportó efectos concluyentes de reducción de glucosa. Los estudios en animales en ratas (2025–2026) mostraron que la L-citrulina moduló la actividad de enzimas pancreáticas y mejoró la sensibilidad a la insulina a través de la síntesis de citrulina derivada de bacterias. Los ensayos humanos verificaron aproximadamente 241 participantes totales, pero la mayoría de los resúmenes carecían de detalles del tamaño de muestra.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Muy pocos ensayos humanos existen, y ningún metanálisis agrupado confirma que coincidan. La evidencia animal es sugestiva pero no predice automáticamente los resultados en humanos. Los datos humanos permanecen preliminares e inconsistentes, justificando una calificación moderada en espera de estudios más grandes o replicados.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Una revisión sistemática de 2020 identificó ensayos sobre citrulina y rendimiento muscular. Ensayos aleatorios recientes (2022–2025) probaron efectos agudos y a 6 semanas: un ensayo aleatorizado de 2025 (n=21) comparó L-citrulina con malato de citrulina en medidas neuromusculares; un ensayo aleatorizado de 2023 examinó efectos agudos en el ejercicio de resistencia y oxigenación muscular en personas entrenadas recreativamente; un ensayo de 2022 (n=13) combinó L-citrulina con entrenamiento de resistencia de velocidad lenta y encontró mejoras en la función endotelial de las piernas. Los tamaños de muestra verificados en 2 de 9 estudios totalizaron solo aproximadamente 34 participantes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Un único metanálisis existe pero no ha sido verificado independientemente. Los tamaños de muestra humana verificados son modestos (aproximadamente 34 en resúmenes publicados). La dirección del efecto es consistente pero la base de evidencia es pequeña y aún no replicada independientemente, manteniendo la calificación en moderada.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La mayor parte de la evidencia es humana y reciente (2019–2026). La mayoría de los ensayos son aleatorios y controlados, variando desde estudios de dosis única aguda hasta intervenciones de 6 semanas. Dos metanálisis independientes respaldan el hallazgo de presión arterial, pero otros resultados dependen de síntesis individuales o ensayos dispersos. Muy pocos estudios a largo plazo (>3 meses) o ensayos a gran escala (>200 participantes por brazo) son visibles en los registros recuperados, lo que significa que la seguridad y eficacia a largo plazo permanecen menos ciertas que los efectos a corto plazo.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados muestran que el rendimiento del ejercicio y la fuerza muscular han sido estudiados solo en adultos sanos o recreativamente activos y personas con síndrome post-COVID-19; la efectividad en adultos mayores frágiles, poblaciones sedentarias o enfermedad crónica permanece sin probar en los resúmenes disponibles. La mayoría de los estudios duran 6 semanas o menos; la seguridad y eficacia más allá de 3 meses no están bien caracterizadas en los datos proporcionados. Los resultados de azúcar en sangre descansan en solo 3 ensayos humanos y hallazgos inconsistentes; si la citrulina realmente mejora el control de glucosa en personas con diabetes o prediabetes no puede ser determinado aún a partir de estos registros. Ningún ensayo recuperado evaluó embarazo, adolescencia o enfermedad renal, dejando la seguridad en estos grupos desconocida.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia de presión arterial es sólida con metanálisis independientes y ~839 participantes verificados; el rendimiento del ejercicio, la fuerza muscular y el azúcar en sangre se basan en ensayos pequeños y heterogéneos sin síntesis combinada, lo que hace prematuros los reclamos clínicos para esos resultados.

concerns.issue: Rendimiento del ejercicio: sin efecto combinado extractable
concerns.detail: A pesar de 19 ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos, el motor señala 'efecto combinado: ninguno extractable.' Existe una única revisión sistemática de 2020, pero permanece sin replicación y sin verificación. Con un tamaño de muestra mediano de 15 y solo 7 de 20 estudios que reportan n, los ensayos individuales carecen de poder estadístico para detectar efectos clínicamente significativos. El ensayo de 2025 'no mejora el rendimiento de carrera en el calor' contradice directamente el beneficio reclamado.

concerns.issue: Fuerza muscular: síntesis escasa y sin verificar
concerns.detail: Solo 9 estudios totales (8 ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos), con efecto combinado 'ninguno extractable.' Solo 2 de 9 estudios reportan tamaños de muestra (n=13, n=21), lo que arroja ~34 participantes verificados en el resultado. El motor señala esto como 'imprecisión: la estimación del efecto puede ser inestable.' Existe una única revisión sistemática de 2020, pero sin replicación independiente. Las conclusiones sobre fuerza muscular se construyen sobre una base de subnotificación severa del tamaño de muestra y dependencia de síntesis única.

concerns.issue: Azúcar en sangre: evidencia predominantemente animal con datos humanos mínimos
concerns.detail: De 13 estudios, 10 son modelos animales; solo 2 son ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos, con n verificado total en humanos ~30 entre ellos. El motor señala 'ningún análisis combinado confirma [que los estudios] concuerdan; mantenido en moderado pendiente de revisión.' Extrapolar de la actividad enzimática pancreática en ratas y el crecimiento fetal en roedores al control de glucosa en humanos es un gran salto mecanístico. La evidencia humana es demasiado escasa y enfocada en animales para apoyar reclamos clínicos.

concerns.issue: Presión arterial: heterogeneidad de resultados y variabilidad del respondedor no resuelta
concerns.detail: Aunque los metanálisis de 2025 y 2019 convergen en una diferencia media de -4,02 mmHg, el ensayo clínico aleatorizado de 2026 (n=66) nota explícitamente que 'los efectos vasculares de la suplementación de L-citrulina en adultos sanos están influenciados en gran medida por la condición preexistente.' Un ensayo de 2026 establece que 'el Cumplimiento y la Variabilidad Genética Son Determinantes del Éxito,' indicando una variación individual sustancial. La estimación combinada oculta subgrupos en quienes el fármaco tiene poco o ningún efecto, y la base de evidencia no identifica claramente predictores de respuesta.

concerns.issue: Subnotificación sistemática de tamaños de muestra en todos los resultados
concerns.detail: En los 70 estudios de la base de evidencia, solo 9–17 de 20–27 por resultado reportan tamaño de muestra, dejando 50–75% de los estudios con n omitido de los resúmenes. El motor reconoce que 'el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor,' pero no puede verificarlo. Esta opacidad impide la evaluación independiente de si la literatura sintetizada tiene poder estadístico adecuado o está sujeta a sesgo de publicación que favorece ensayos pequeños positivos. Los lectores no pueden evaluar la precisión real de las estimaciones combinadas.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: L-Citrulina → producción aumentada de NO → vasodilatación endotelial → presión arterial más baja es coherente biológicamente y está apoyado por la evidencia de presión arterial (dos metanálisis, ~839 participantes). Sin embargo, el salto de la biodisponibilidad de NO al rendimiento del ejercicio y la fuerza muscular es más débil: el NO mejora el flujo sanguíneo, pero si esto se traduce en ganancias medibles en fuerza de resistencia o capacidad de trabajo aeróbico en poblaciones entrenadas o no entrenadas sigue siendo poco claro en los ensayos clínicos aleatorizados recuperados. Los efectos sobre el azúcar en sangre se derivan puramente de animales (modulación de enzimas pancreáticas, programación fetal), sin puente mecanístico demostrado en los 2 pequeños ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Para el rendimiento del ejercicio y la fuerza muscular, un escéptico señalaría que los 16–19 ensayos clínicos aleatorizados recuperados muestran n mediano=13–21, no existe agrupamiento metaanalítico para ninguno de los dos resultados, y un ensayo de 2025 explícitamente *no encuentra* mejora en el rendimiento de carrera. Las calificaciones 'Moderada' se basan en revisiones sistemáticas únicas y sin replicación escritas antes de que la mayoría de los datos de 2025–2026 llegaran. Para el azúcar en sangre, el 77% de la evidencia es trabajo animal; los 2 ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos son diminutos e insuficientemente potentes. La calificación 'Moderada' allí es principalmente un marcador de posición en lugar de una declaración de confianza. En general, solo la presión arterial supera un umbral alto; los otros tres resultados han sido mejorados para coincidir con su prominencia en el marketing sin apoyo empírico equivalente.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Para el rendimiento del ejercicio y la fuerza muscular: un ensayo clínico aleatorizado multicéntrico con n≥150, resultado primario preespecificado (p. ej., 1-RM en prensa de piernas, tiempo hasta el agotamiento en sujetos entrenados) y protocolo publicado resolvería la heterogeneidad; alternativamente, un metanálisis registrado con métodos modernos (p. ej., estratificación de riesgo de sesgo, análisis de subgrupos por estado de entrenamiento) podría aclarar el tamaño del efecto real. Para el azúcar en sangre: un ensayo clínico aleatorizado adecuadamente potente (n≥200) en personas con prediabetes o diabetes tipo 2, midiendo HbA1c como resultado primario durante ≥12 semanas, movería la evidencia de dominada por animales a basada en humanos. Para la presión arterial, el panorama ya es razonablemente claro; el siguiente paso es identificar predictores de respondedores (genéticos, metabólicos, estado de presión arterial basal) para pasar de promedios poblacionales a medicina de precisión.
